products.title: One ESP32 core, a device for every job

decisions.title: The hard parts, solved on purpose

items.title: No reading is lost
items.body: Offline readings are buffered in flash and replayed with their original time. Ingest ignores duplicates by sequence number.

items.title: Commands you can trust
items.body: Every switch shows sent, delivered and confirmed by the device, or a clear timeout. Never a button that pretends.

items.title: Alerts without spam
items.body: Rules wait out short spikes, clear with a margin so they can't flap, and respect a cool-down and quiet hours.

items.title: Updates can't brick a box
items.body: Signed firmware goes to the spare partition and is kept only if the node checks in. Otherwise it rolls back.

security.title: A device can only speak for itself
security.lead: Connected equipment is a way into a network. Nabd treats every node as untrusted until it proves who it is.

items.title: Encrypted end to end
items.body: TLS on MQTT, HTTPS and WebSocket. Nothing travels in plain text.

items.title: One key per device
items.body: Broker rules let each node publish and listen only under its own topic.

items.title: Signed firmware
items.body: A node refuses any update that isn't signed with the release key.

items.title: Every action logged
items.body: Who switched what, when, and what the device answered.

architecture.title: How a reading moves through Nabd

products.lead: One ESP32-S3 core, many jobs. Every Nabd device shares the same firmware, security and dashboard, so a fridge probe and a pump controller behave the same way.
products.elseBody: Every node is open hardware. Pick a sensor and the firmware has a driver slot for it.

kitPoints: Flash and provision in about 10 minutes
Appears live on the demo fleet

shares.title: Open protocols
shares.body: MQTT over TLS, a published topic contract and JSON payloads. Any broker or platform can read them.

shares.title: Offline memory
shares.body: 5,000 readings kept in flash during a Wi-Fi drop, replayed in order with their original timestamps.

shares.title: Secure by default
shares.body: Pinned broker certificate, a unique key per device and firmware that must carry a valid signature.

shares.title: Remote updates
shares.body: Two firmware slots. A new version is kept only after the node checks in; otherwise it rolls back.

shares.title: Readable on the box
shares.body: A small screen shows readings, connection state and the last command, so a technician needs no phone.

shares.title: Safe when alone
shares.body: Relays switch off if the link is lost for too long, and a watchdog restarts a stuck node.

faq.q: Is the hardware real or only a design?
faq.a: Prototypes are one ESP32-S3 board with off-the-shelf sensors, running the same firmware with a different device profile; one P1 reports to the live demo. The enclosures pictured are AI concept renders. Products marked Planned are designed but not built yet.

faq.q: Can I use my own sensors?
faq.a: Yes. The firmware has a small driver interface: add a sensor, map its readings to metric names in the shared registry, and the dashboard, alerts and history work without other changes.

faq.q: What happens when the internet goes down?
faq.a: The node keeps sampling and stores up to 5,000 readings in flash. When the connection returns it sends them in order with their original timestamps, so charts have no gaps.
Firmware must be signed with the release key. The node installs it to a spare slot and only keeps it after it reconnects and publishes successfully; otherwise it rolls back by itself.

faq.q: Do the planned BLE tags need a special gateway?
faq.a: They report through the G1 gateway, which reads standard iBeacon and Eddystone advertising, so third-party BLE sensor tags using those formats can work too.
